periods.activity_title: What does food do inside us?
periods.activity_description: Students examine everyday observations — why chewed chapati tastes sweeter, what happens when we hold our breath — and record these as phenomena that need explaining. They sort their observations into two columns: things they notice about eating and digestion, and things they notice about breathing and energy.

roles.role_description: Prompts students with guiding questions drawn from familiar food and breathing experiences, then facilitates sharing of observations.
Record personal observations about eating, digestion, and breathing in a two-column table.
Compare their individual observations and identify which phenomena are shared across the group.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses two anchor questions: why does chewed rice taste sweeter than unchewed rice, and what happens to the oxygen we breathe in — students think silently and jot initial ideas.
Students individually record observations about eating and digestion in one column and about breathing and energy in a second column, drawing on personal experience.
Small groups compare their columns, circling observations that appear in at least two members' notes and flagging any disagreements.
Whole-class share-out of two or three standout observations; teacher records them on the board as an open question bank for the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit sets up the chapter's two main phenomena — nutrition and respiration — as puzzles rooted in students' own experience, so resist the urge to explain anything yet. Watch for students who conflate digestion with simply eating: they may say 'food gives energy' without connecting that to any breakdown process. A useful checkpoint is whether students can name at least one observation they genuinely cannot yet explain — that curiosity gap is what the following units will fill.

periods.activity_description: Students test boiled rice for starch using iodine solution, comparing a sample of unchewed rice with rice that has been thoroughly chewed in the mouth, and record the colour change observed in each sample to identify where starch breakdown begins.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the iodine test on one sample, then circulates to ensure students handle iodine solution safely and record observations accurately.
Carry out the iodine test on both rice samples, record colour changes, and write one sentence describing what the colour difference tells them about the unchewed versus chewed sample.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the previous unit's open question about chewed rice tasting sweeter, then demonstrates the iodine test on a small portion of unchewed boiled rice.
Student groups chew a small portion of boiled rice for an extended period, then test both the unchewed and chewed samples with iodine solution and record the colour outcome for each.
Groups write one sentence explaining what the colour difference indicates about starch in each sample, using only their observation as evidence.
Whole-class comparison of results; teacher asks groups whose results differ to describe their procedure so the class can identify sources of variation.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit grounds the abstract idea of chemical digestion in a direct, student-produced observation, building on the open question bank from the previous unit. A common error is that students dip iodine into the unchewed sample but forget to wait long enough before reading the colour — remind them the colour shift needs a moment to appear. If results vary across groups, treat this as productive data rather than failure: ask groups to compare how long they chewed to see whether chewing time affected the outcome.

periods.stage_label: Trace and sequence the pathway of digestion
periods.activity_description: Students trace the sequential journey of a mouthful of food from mouth to anus, labelling each organ of the alimentary canal and recording the specific transformation food undergoes at each station, producing a completed pathway diagram in their notebooks.

roles.role_description: Narrates the journey of food organ by organ, pausing at each station to pose a focusing question about what that organ contributes before students label and annotate.
Draw a simplified linear diagram of the alimentary canal and annotate each organ with the type of digestion occurring and the substance acted upon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit's iodine activity by asking: if starch breakdown starts in the mouth, what must happen to the other components of food — proteins and fats — and where?

Teacher narrates the journey station by station — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine — pausing after each organ so students annotate their diagram with the transformation occurring there.
Students review their completed diagrams and write one sentence for each organ that begins with a substance entering and ends with a product leaving.
Teacher conducts a quick whole-class check by naming an organ and asking students to call out what enters and what leaves, correcting any sequencing errors heard.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves students from isolated observation to an ordered sequence — the alimentary canal as a single connected system — which is a significant cognitive step from the previous two units. Watch for students who treat the stomach as the sole site of digestion and overlook the small intestine's central role in both digestion and absorption; this is the most common sequencing error in this chapter. A useful probe is to ask why the small intestine needs to be six metres long — if students can connect length to surface area and absorption, they are tracking the sequence correctly.
materials: Blackboard diagram of the alimentary canal

periods.stage_label: Trace and sequence the pathway of digestion
periods.activity_description: Student groups investigate how ruminants and birds digest food without teeth, using chapter information about rumination and the gizzard to construct a comparison table that maps feeding strategy to digestive structure and explains why each adaptation works.

roles.role_description: Poses the driving question — if teeth are essential for breaking food in humans, how do toothless animals manage — then circulates to probe groups whose comparisons remain at the descriptive level.
Build a three-column comparison table (animal, digestive structure, how it replaces the function of teeth) and then write one explanatory sentence per animal linking structure to function.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the driving question and asks students to predict, before consulting their notes, what a cow or a bird might do instead of chewing with teeth.
Groups build the comparison table using the chapter information on ruminants and birds, completing all three columns for each animal.
Each group writes one explanatory sentence per animal that connects the structure described to the function that teeth perform in humans.
Two groups share their sentences; class discusses whether the explanation goes beyond naming the structure to explaining why it works.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the human digestive sequence; this unit asks students to reason about variation on that theme, which demands functional rather than purely descriptive thinking. Students often describe rumination as simply 'chewing again' without connecting it to the fact that grasses are tough to break down chemically and need extended mechanical processing — press them to say why the cow benefits from returning food to the mouth. If groups finish the table quickly, ask them to predict what would happen to a bird that swallowed food without access to small stones.
materials: Chapter summary or textbook pages on ruminants and birds

periods.stage_label: Observe and trace the pathway of respiration
periods.activity_description: Students construct or observe a model made from a plastic bottle and balloons that simulates the effect of diaphragm and rib movement on lung volume, recording what happens to the inner balloons when the outer membrane is pulled down versus pushed up.

roles.role_description: Leads construction or demonstration of the bottle-and-balloon model, directing student attention to the relationship between the outer membrane's movement and the inner balloons' inflation.
Manipulate the model, record observations of what happens to the inner balloons under each membrane position, and draw a two-state diagram labelled 'inhalation' and 'exhalation'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the respiratory system briefly, recalling the question from unit one about what happens to the oxygen we breathe in, then presents the bottle-and-balloon model components.
Groups assemble or interact with the model, pulling and pushing the outer membrane repeatedly while a recorder in each group notes the change in the inner balloon size for each membrane position.
Students draw a two-state diagram showing the chest cavity during inhalation and exhalation, labelling the diaphragm, ribs, and lungs in each state.
Teacher asks each group to describe their diagram using only the words 'volume increases/decreases' and 'air moves in/out' to check whether they have connected cavity volume to airflow direction.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the respiration arc and deliberately mirrors the hands-on approach used in unit two, helping students recognise that 'doing science' applies equally to both major life processes in the chapter. The most persistent misconception here is that the lungs actively push themselves to expand — students must come to see that the lungs are passive and that it is the surrounding cavity's volume change that drives airflow; probe this by asking 'what would happen to the balloons if we cut them free from the bottle?' If the model construction is time-consuming, prepare assembled models in advance so groups can focus their energy on observation and diagramming.
materials: One large balloon or rubber sheet (outer membrane)

periods.stage_label: Observe and trace the pathway of respiration
periods.activity_title: What is in exhaled air? — Activity 9.3
periods.activity_description: Teacher demonstrates that exhaled air turns lime water milky while inhaled air does not, and students record the composition data for inhaled versus exhaled air before producing a labelled diagram of gas exchange at the alveoli.

roles.role_description: Performs the lime water demonstration for inhaled and exhaled air, then presents the percentage composition figures for inhaled and exhaled air and guides students through a labelled alveolus diagram.
Record the lime water results, note the percentage figures for both air types, and complete a labelled diagram showing the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement across the alveolus wall.

time_bands.activity: Teacher performs the lime water test — first blowing exhaled air through lime water, then drawing fresh air through it — and students record what they observe in each case.

Teacher presents the composition figures for inhaled air (21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide) and exhaled air (16-17% oxygen, 4-5% carbon dioxide); students record these and calculate the approximate change in each gas.
Students draw and label an alveolus diagram showing the blood vessel, the alveolus wall, and the arrows indicating the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement during gas exchange.
Teacher asks students to write the word equation for respiration below their diagram and to circle which substance on the left side of the equation was tracked by the lime water test.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the model work of the previous unit: the bottle-and-balloon showed how air moves; this demonstration shows what that air carries and what happens to it at the alveolus. The most important distinction to reinforce is between breathing (physical air movement) and respiration (chemical reaction at the cell level) — many students use the two words interchangeably, so explicitly name the difference when introducing the word equation. If lime water is unavailable, the demonstration can be replaced with a description of Activity 9.3 followed by the composition data alone, though the visual impact of the milky change is worth preparing for.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking life processes
periods.activity_title: Why does the body need both digestion and respiration?
periods.activity_description: Student groups construct a cause-and-effect chain connecting the digestion of food in the alimentary canal to the production of glucose, the transport of glucose to cells, and the release of energy through cellular respiration using the word equation, explaining why both processes are essential for the animal to function.

roles.role_description: Poses the integrating question — what would happen to an animal that could digest food perfectly but could not carry out respiration — and circulates to challenge groups that produce a chain without causal connectives.

Construct a written cause-and-effect chain of at least five linked steps from 'food enters the mouth' to 'energy is available to the cell', using causal language such as 'so that', 'because', and 'which allows'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the integrating question and asks groups to predict the answer before building the chain, recording their prediction as a single sentence to revisit at the end of the unit.
Groups construct the cause-and-effect chain in writing, ensuring each step is connected to the next with an explicit causal connective and that both digestion and respiration are represented.
Groups compare their chain to their opening prediction and write one sentence on whether their prediction was accurate and what they now understand that they did not before building the chain.
Two groups read their chains aloud; class identifies any steps where a link is missing or where a connective is merely sequential ('then') rather than causal ('so that', 'because').

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the first moment students are asked to reason across both life processes rather than within each one separately, marking the transition to the chapter's highest cognitive demand. Watch for chains that are sequential lists — 'food goes to the stomach, then to the small intestine, then glucose goes to the blood' — without any causal language explaining why each step matters; the presence of 'so that' or 'because' is your signal that a group has moved from sequencing to causal reasoning. The integrating question about a perfectly digesting but non-respiring animal is a useful probe: if students say 'it would starve' they are still thinking only about digestion, but if they say 'it would have glucose but no way to release energy from it' they have grasped the dependency.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking life processes
periods.activity_title: Respiratory diversity — from gills to skin
periods.activity_description: Teacher explains how fish, frogs, and earthworms obtain oxygen through structures other than lungs, and students construct a structured comparison that explains why each respiratory structure suits the animal's environment, extending the causal reasoning framework built in the previous unit.

roles.role_description: Explains gill, amphibian, and skin-based respiration in turn, pausing after each to ask students to articulate the environmental condition that makes that structure functional.
Complete a structured table with columns for animal, respiratory structure, environment, and one causal sentence explaining why the structure works in that environment.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to recall the cause-and-effect chain from the previous unit and identify which step — gas exchange — is the one that different animals solve differently.

Teacher explains gill respiration in fish, dual-mode respiration in frogs (gills as tadpoles, lungs and moist skin as adults), and skin-based gas exchange in earthworms, pausing after each for students to complete their table row.

Students write one causal sentence per animal that begins with the environmental condition and ends with why the respiratory structure is functional there — for example, 'because earthworms live in moist soil, their skin can stay wet enough for gas to dissolve and diffuse across it'.
Teacher invites two or three students to read their causal sentences; class evaluates whether each sentence names an environmental condition, a structural feature, and a functional outcome.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the causal reasoning framework from the previous unit into cross-species comparison, requiring students to apply the same logic — structure fits environment — to unfamiliar cases. A common error is that students describe the frog as 'using both gills and lungs at the same time' rather than understanding that gills function in the tadpole stage and lungs develop for life on land, with moist skin providing a supplementary route; clarify the life-stage dimension explicitly. Encouraging students to use the sentence frame 'because [environment], [structure] works by [mechanism]' will help weaker writers produce genuinely causal rather than merely descriptive responses.

periods.stage_label: Apply causal reasoning to explain how life processes sustain animal life
periods.activity_title: What happens when a life process fails?
periods.activity_description: Students analyse three scenario cards describing disruptions to digestion or respiration in different animals and explain, using causal reasoning, how each disruption cascades through connected life processes to threaten the animal's survival, applying their understanding of the full chapter to novel cases.

roles.role_description: Distributes scenario cards and frames the task as applying the chapter's causal framework to novel problems, circulating to ensure students identify which life process is disrupted and trace the downstream consequence.
Analyse each scenario, identify the disrupted life process, trace the causal chain of consequences, and write a justified explanation of why the disruption threatens the animal's survival.
Write a final synthesis sentence connecting both major life processes covered in the chapter to the shared goal of sustaining animal life.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes scenario cards — one describing a blocked small intestine, one describing collapsed alveoli, one describing a fish removed from water — and asks groups to read all three before beginning.
Groups analyse each scenario by identifying the disrupted process, writing a causal chain of consequences, and producing one sentence explaining why survival is threatened.
Each student individually writes one synthesis sentence that names both nutrition and respiration and connects them to a single shared outcome — the sustaining of animal life.

Three groups share their analysis of one scenario each; class evaluates whether each explanation identifies a specific disrupted process and traces a consequence rather than merely restating the scenario.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to transfer the causal reasoning developed across the chapter to three novel scenarios, which is the chapter's highest cognitive demand and the operation named in the chapter's dissolution test. The fish-removed-from-water scenario is the most challenging because it requires students to connect the environmental dependency of gill function to the broader consequence of no gas exchange — watch for groups who simply say 'the fish can't breathe' without explaining the mechanism. The individual synthesis sentence is a useful exit-level signal: a strong sentence names both processes and their functional relationship, whereas a weak one names them without connecting them to any shared outcome.
materials: Scenario cards (three per group, prepared in advance)

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe everyday phenomena related to digestion and breathing, record them systematically, and carry out the iodine-starch test to detect where starch breakdown begins in the alimentary canal.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe at least two observable phenomena associated with digestion and breathing, and report the result of the iodine test on chewed versus unchewed rice with a one-sentence interpretation.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Trace and sequence the pathway of digestion
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sequence the organs of the alimentary canal and annotate each with its digestive function, then compare digestive strategies across humans, ruminants, and birds by mapping structure to function.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can sequence the organs of the human alimentary canal, state the transformation food undergoes at each organ, and explain how at least one non-human digestive structure performs the same function as teeth in humans.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and trace the pathway of respiration
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students model chest cavity volume changes driving airflow, observe the lime water test for carbon dioxide in exhaled air, record the composition of inhaled versus exhaled air, and label the direction of gas exchange across the alveolus.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how diaphragm and rib movement drives inhalation and exhalation, state the composition difference between inhaled and exhaled air, and produce a labelled diagram showing the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement across the alveolus.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking life processes
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct cause-and-effect chains connecting digestion to cellular respiration, then explain how gill, amphibian, and skin-based respiration each suit the animal's environment using causal language.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a causal chain connecting food intake through digestion and absorption to energy release via cellular respiration, and write one causal sentence per non-human respiratory structure explaining why it functions in that animal's environment.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply causal reasoning to explain how life processes sustain animal life
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse novel disruption scenarios for digestion and respiration in different animals, trace the causal consequences for survival, and write a synthesis statement connecting both life processes to the sustaining of animal life.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply their understanding of nutrition and respiration to explain, using causal reasoning, how a disruption to either process threatens an animal's survival, and can articulate how both processes together sustain animal life.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe at least two observable phenomena associated with digestion and breathing, and report the result of the iodine test on chewed versus unchewed rice with a one-sentence interpretation.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: A student chews boiled rice for an extended period and then tests both the unchewed and chewed samples with iodine solution. The unchewed sample turns blue-black. What result would the chewed sample most likely show, and what does it indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: The chewed sample also turns blue-black, indicating that chewing does not affect starch.

options.label: B
options.text: The chewed sample shows little or no blue-black colour, indicating that starch has been broken down in the mouth.

options.label: C
options.text: The chewed sample turns red, indicating that a new acid has been produced by the salivary glands.

options.label: D
options.text: The chewed sample turns yellow, indicating that iodine reacts differently with saliva than with starch.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student believes mechanical chewing is the only action in the mouth and does not register that saliva contains a chemical agent that breaks down starch.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the chemical action of saliva with acid production, misattributing the stomach's function to the mouth.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has no functional model of the iodine test and treats colour change as an arbitrary reaction rather than a specific indicator for starch.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the iodine test procedure can still demonstrate this outcome by reasoning from the observation that chewed chapati tastes sweeter — both pathways evidence the same understanding that starch breaks down in the mouth. Allowing students to draw the two test tubes and shade the colour they expect is an equally valid demonstration.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe at least two observable phenomena associated with digestion and breathing, and report the result of the iodine test on chewed versus unchewed rice with a one-sentence interpretation.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: Which of the following correctly describes what iodine solution is used for in Activity 9.1, and why the result differs between the two rice samples?

options.label: A
options.text: Iodine tests for the presence of protein; the chewed sample has less protein because saliva digests it.

options.label: B
options.text: Iodine tests for the presence of glucose; the unchewed sample has more glucose because starch converts to glucose in unbroken rice.

options.label: C
options.text: Iodine tests for the presence of starch; the chewed sample shows less starch because the salivary digestive juice breaks it down during chewing.

options.label: D
options.text: Iodine tests for the presence of starch; both samples show the same result because the stomach, not the mouth, digests starch.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the role of saliva with protein digestion, which is actually the stomach's function, and misidentifies what iodine detects.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student knows that starch converts to sugar but inverts the direction — believing unbroken rice has more glucose — and misidentifies the substance that iodine tests for.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly identifies iodine as a starch test but holds the misconception that digestion of starch begins in the stomach rather than the mouth.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the chemistry can still access this question by recalling the taste observation — chewed rice becomes sweeter — and reasoning backward to what must be disappearing. Allowing a paired discussion before individual answer selection widens access without reducing cognitive demand.

assessment_items.stage_label: Trace and sequence the pathway of digestion
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sequence the organs of the human alimentary canal, state the transformation food undergoes at each organ, and explain how at least one non-human digestive structure performs the same function as teeth in humans.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'The small intestine only absorbs food — it does not digest it.' Which of the following most accurately corrects this statement?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct: digestion is complete by the time food leaves the stomach, and the small intestine only absorbs.

options.label: B
options.text: The small intestine both digests and absorbs: it receives secretions from its own lining, the liver, and the pancreas to further break down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, and then absorbs nutrients through its finger-like projections.

options.label: C
options.text: The small intestine digests food but does not absorb it — absorption happens in the large intestine where water and salts are taken up.

options.label: D
options.text: The small intestine only digests fats using bile; the pancreas separately absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student holds the very misconception the question is designed to probe — that digestion ends in the stomach — and has not registered the small intestine's digestive role.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the large intestine's function (water and salt absorption) with the small intestine's absorption function, inverting where nutrient absorption occurs.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has partial knowledge of bile's role in fat digestion but incorrectly assigns the pancreas an absorption function and limits the small intestine to fat digestion only.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to hold the full sequence in working memory can be asked to sketch a simple arrow diagram of the canal before answering, externalising the sequence so they can evaluate the options against it. Peer explanation — asking a student to tell a partner what leaves the stomach — is another valid access route.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sequence the organs of the human alimentary canal, state the transformation food undergoes at each organ, and explain how at least one non-human digestive structure performs the same function as teeth in humans.

assessment_items.question_text: Birds do not have teeth. Which structure in a bird's digestive system performs the mechanical breakdown of food that teeth perform in humans, and how does it do so?

options.label: A
options.text: The oesophagus; it churns food with strong muscular contractions before passing it to the stomach.

options.label: B
options.text: The gizzard; its powerful muscular walls contract and grind food, sometimes aided by small stones the bird has swallowed.

options.label: C
options.text: The stomach; it secretes extra acid that chemically dissolves food particles, replacing the need for teeth entirely.

options.label: D
options.text: The large intestine; it compresses undigested material so tightly that food particles are broken into smaller pieces.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the oesophagus's role — a muscular passage for moving food — with a digestive function it does not perform, likely because the chapter mentions the oesophagus's wave-like contractions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student conflates chemical digestion (acid in the stomach) with mechanical digestion and incorrectly assigns the function of teeth replacement to stomach acid.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has misapplied the large intestine's compression of waste material to a mechanical digestion role, confusing egestion with digestion.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot recall the gizzard by name can still reason to the correct option by eliminating structures whose functions they know (oesophagus moves food, large intestine handles waste) — explicitly teaching elimination as a strategy supports students who struggle with recall-under-pressure.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sequence the organs of the human alimentary canal, state the transformation food undergoes at each organ, and explain how at least one non-human digestive structure performs the same function as teeth in humans.

assessment_items.question_text: A cow swallows grass quickly without chewing it fully, then later returns it to its mouth to chew it again. Name this process and explain why it is necessary for cows but not for humans.
expected_elements: Names the process as rumination or chewing the cud.
States that the cow swallows partially chewed grass and stores it in part of the stomach before returning it to the mouth.
Identifies that grasses are tough and require extended mechanical processing that a single chewing episode cannot achieve.
Contrasts this with humans, whose diet does not require repeated mechanical breakdown of the same food mass.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who cannot write the explanation in full sentences can be invited to draw a two-step diagram — grass swallowed, then returned to mouth — and label what changes at each step. The diagram pathway evidences the same sequencing and functional reasoning as written prose.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and trace the pathway of respiration
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how diaphragm and rib movement drives inhalation and exhalation, state the composition difference between inhaled and exhaled air, and produce a labelled diagram showing the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement across the alveolus.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: During inhalation, the ribs move upward and outward and the diaphragm moves downward. What does this do to the volume of the chest cavity, and how does that cause air to enter the lungs?

options.label: A
options.text: The volume decreases, squeezing the lungs so they push air inward through the nostrils.

options.label: B
options.text: The volume increases, creating a lower pressure inside the chest so that air from outside rushes into the lungs.

options.label: C
options.text: The volume stays the same, but the diaphragm actively pumps air into the lungs by moving up and down.

options.label: D
options.text: The volume increases, but air enters only because the nostrils widen to let more air pass through.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has the direction of the rib and diaphragm movement correct but inverts the volume-pressure relationship, believing the chest squeezes inward during inhalation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student holds the misconception that the diaphragm actively pumps air rather than understanding that it changes cavity volume, which passively draws air in.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly identifies that volume increases but attributes airflow to nostril widening rather than the pressure difference created by the volume change.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to visualise the cavity can be directed to recall the bottle-and-balloon model: pulling the outer membrane down expanded the inner balloons. Connecting the abstract concept to the physical model they manipulated provides an alternative reasoning pathway to the same answer.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how diaphragm and rib movement drives inhalation and exhalation, state the composition difference between inhaled and exhaled air, and produce a labelled diagram showing the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement across the alveolus.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Air type | Approximate oxygen (%) | Approximate carbon dioxide (%)
Inhaled air | 21 | 0.04
Exhaled air | 16-17 | 4-5
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student blows exhaled air through lime water and observes it turns milky, but when fresh air is drawn through a second container of lime water, it remains clear. Which conclusion is best supported by the table data and this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Lime water detects oxygen; because exhaled air has less oxygen, it turns lime water milky.

options.label: B
options.text: Exhaled air contains significantly more carbon dioxide than inhaled air, and it is this carbon dioxide that turns lime water milky.

options.label: C
options.text: Exhaled air contains significantly less oxygen than inhaled air, so lime water turns milky because it reacts with the absence of oxygen.

options.label: D
options.text: Both inhaled and exhaled air contain carbon dioxide, so lime water should turn milky in both containers equally.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates oxygen with carbon dioxide as the substance lime water detects, possibly because oxygen is the more prominent gas discussed in respiration contexts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies that exhaled air has less oxygen but constructs an incoherent causal claim — that the absence of a substance causes a chemical reaction — reflecting a gap in understanding what lime water actually reacts with.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly notes that both air types contain carbon dioxide but ignores the quantitative difference shown in the table, leading to the incorrect prediction of equal milkiness.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the percentage figures difficult to interpret can be redirected to the simpler observation: one container turned milky and one did not — what changed between the two tests? This reasoning-from-observation pathway reaches the same conclusion without requiring interpretation of the full table.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and trace the pathway of respiration
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how diaphragm and rib movement drives inhalation and exhalation, state the composition difference between inhaled and exhaled air, and produce a labelled diagram showing the direction of oxygen and carbon dioxide movement across the alveolus.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: At the alveolus, blood arriving from the body's cells carries carbon dioxide and returns with oxygen. Describe the direction of movement of each gas across the alveolus wall and explain what drives each gas to move in the direction it does.
expected_elements: States that carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air inside the alveolus.
States that oxygen moves from the air inside the alveolus into the blood.
Identifies that carbon dioxide moves out because it is at a higher concentration in the blood arriving from body cells.
Identifies that oxygen moves in because it is at a higher concentration in the freshly inhaled air in the alveolus.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find written description difficult can draw the alveolus with blood vessels on either side and add directional arrows for each gas, labelling the arrow with the gas name. A correctly arrowed and labelled diagram demonstrates the same directional and causal understanding as a written response.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms linking life processes
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a causal chain connecting food intake through digestion and absorption to energy release via cellular respiration, and write one causal sentence per non-human respiratory structure explaining why it functions in that animal's environment.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: An earthworm has no lungs or gills, yet it can carry out respiration. Which of the following best explains how this is possible and what environmental condition is essential for the mechanism to work?

options.label: A
options.text: The earthworm absorbs oxygen through its intestine wall; it must live in soil rich in organic matter to supply enough oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: The earthworm exchanges gases through its moist skin surface; the skin must remain wet so that oxygen and carbon dioxide can dissolve and diffuse across it.

options.label: C
options.text: The earthworm uses gills hidden inside its body segments; it must live in wet soil so the gills stay functional.

options.label: D
options.text: The earthworm breathes through tiny holes in its outer surface that open directly to the bloodstream; these holes close if the soil dries out.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the site of gas exchange (skin) with the site of nutrient absorption (intestine), possibly because both involve diffusion through a body surface.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student applies the concept of gills to the earthworm, likely because gills and moist-skin respiration are both associated with aquatic or semi-aquatic environments in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates the earthworm's skin-based gas exchange with the spiracle-based system of insects, inventing a structural detail not present in the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot recall the specific mechanism can be prompted to reason from elimination: the chapter names lungs, gills, and moist skin as the three mechanisms, and the earthworm is explicitly described as lacking specialised organs — which of the three options does that leave? This elimination pathway reaches the answer without requiring direct recall.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a causal chain connecting food intake through digestion and absorption to energy release via cellular respiration, and write one causal sentence per non-human respiratory structure explaining why it functions in that animal's environment.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'Digestion and respiration are completely separate processes — digestion happens in the alimentary canal and respiration happens in the lungs, so they have nothing to do with each other.' Which of the following best identifies the flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct that they are separate processes, but wrong about location — respiration actually occurs in the alimentary canal as well.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is wrong because digestion and respiration share the same organ — the small intestine carries out both digestion and gas exchange simultaneously.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is wrong because digestion produces glucose that is absorbed into the blood and transported to cells, where it is used as the fuel for cellular respiration to release energy — the two processes are causally linked.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is wrong only about location — respiration does not occur in the lungs but in the liver, which is where glucose is converted to energy.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student accepts the student's flawed premise and only disputes location, showing that they have not grasped the functional relationship between the two processes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recognises that the two processes must be connected but incorrectly locates the connection in a shared organ rather than in the substrate (glucose) that one process produces for the other.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly challenges the location claim but replaces one error with another — assigning cellular respiration to the liver — indicating a partial but unresolved understanding of where energy release occurs.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract causal link can be asked to re-read the word equation (Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy) and identify where glucose comes from — this grounds the abstract claim in a concrete equation they worked with in units seven and eight.

assessment_items.question_text: A frog breathes through gills as a tadpole and through lungs and moist skin as an adult. Explain why this change in respiratory structure occurs and identify the environmental condition that makes moist-skin gas exchange possible for the adult frog.
expected_elements: States that the tadpole lives in water and uses gills to extract dissolved oxygen from the water.
States that the adult frog moves onto land, where gills are no longer functional because there is no surrounding water to extract dissolved oxygen from.
States that the adult frog develops lungs to breathe air on land.
Identifies moist skin as an additional gas exchange surface available to the adult frog when in water.
States that the skin must remain moist because gases must dissolve in water to diffuse across the skin surface.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who cannot produce a full written explanation can be invited to draw a life-cycle diagram of the frog with labelled respiratory structures at each stage and an annotation indicating the environmental condition required. The diagram and annotation pathway demonstrates the same causal and environmental reasoning.

assessment_items.stage_label: Apply causal reasoning to explain how life processes sustain animal life
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can apply their understanding of nutrition and respiration to explain, using causal reasoning, how a disruption to either process threatens an animal's survival, and can articulate how both processes together sustain animal life.

competency.competency_text: Distinguishing the characteristics of living organisms including need for nutrition, growth and development, need for respiration, response to stimuli, reproduction, excretion, and cellular organisation.

assessment_items.question_text: A fish is removed from water and placed in a dry container. Even though the fish has gills, it cannot obtain oxygen from the air. Which of the following best explains why the fish's gills cannot function in air?

options.label: A
options.text: Gills are too small to process the large volume of air needed for breathing, so the fish does not get enough oxygen.

options.label: B
options.text: Gills are designed to extract dissolved oxygen from water; in air, oxygen is not dissolved in a liquid medium, so it cannot diffuse across the gill surface into the blood.

options.label: C
options.text: Air contains too much oxygen for gills to process safely, causing them to shut down to protect the fish.

options.label: D
options.text: Gills work by moving water past their surface; without the movement of water, there is no pressure to push oxygen into the blood.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student focuses on a physical size or capacity argument rather than understanding that the mechanism of gill gas exchange depends on oxygen being dissolved in water, not on volume.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student inverts the problem — imagining air has too much oxygen — rather than recognising that the issue is the state in which oxygen must be presented for diffusion to occur.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student partially understands that water movement is involved in gill function but attributes the mechanism to pressure rather than to the requirement that oxygen be dissolved in a liquid medium.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the diffusion concept abstract can be redirected to the earthworm's moist-skin requirement — both mechanisms share the same principle that gases must dissolve in a liquid to cross a biological surface. Making this cross-animal connection supports students who grasped the earthworm case to transfer the reasoning to fish.

assessment_items.question_text: If the alveoli in a person's lungs collapsed completely, which of the following consequences would follow most directly, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The person would be unable to digest proteins because the pancreas secretes its juice into the alveoli for distribution to cells.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxygen could not pass into the blood, so cells throughout the body would receive no oxygen for cellular respiration and could not release energy from glucose.

options.label: C
options.text: The diaphragm would stop moving because it receives its signal to contract from the alveoli, so breathing would cease immediately.

options.label: D
options.text: Carbon dioxide would accumulate only in the lungs, because without alveoli to release it, the gas would remain stored in the chest cavity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student conflates the alveoli with a distribution system for digestive secretions, indicating a fundamental confusion between the respiratory and digestive systems.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student correctly identifies that breathing would be affected but inverts the causal direction — the diaphragm drives airflow to the alveoli, not the other way around.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student understands that carbon dioxide removal is disrupted but incorrectly locates the consequence in the lungs rather than understanding that carbon dioxide would accumulate in the blood and cells throughout the body.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who cannot reconstruct the causal chain from memory can be prompted with the word equation — Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy — and asked which input on the left side would be missing if alveoli collapsed. This equation-anchored approach provides a structured entry point to the same reasoning.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can apply their understanding of nutrition and respiration to explain, using causal reasoning, how a disruption to either process threatens an animal's survival, and can articulate how both processes together sustain animal life.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'If an animal eats plenty of food and digests it well, it has everything it needs to survive.' Using your understanding of nutrition and respiration as life processes, explain why this statement is incomplete and what else the animal must be able to do to sustain life.
look_for: Identifies that digestion produces glucose and other absorbed nutrients but does not release energy directly.
Explains that the animal must also carry out cellular respiration — using oxygen to react with glucose — to release the energy stored in glucose.
Makes an explicit causal link: without respiration, glucose cannot be converted to usable energy and life processes cannot continue.
Uses the word equation or its components (glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, energy) to support the argument.
Articulates that nutrition and respiration are both necessary and that neither alone is sufficient to sustain life.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing challenging can be supported by offering a sentence-starter framework: 'Digestion produces _____, but to release energy the animal must also _____. Without _____, the animal cannot _____ because _____.' This framework channels the same causal reasoning through a more structured written form without reducing the cognitive demand.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Life process disrupted | Structure or organ affected | Immediate consequence | Why survival is threatened
A cow's rumen is blocked and food cannot be returned to the mouth for re-chewing | | | |
A person's small intestine finger-like projections are damaged and cannot absorb nutrients | | | |
A frog's skin dries out completely while it is resting in shallow water | | | |
A bird swallows food but its gizzard stops contracting | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each scenario: (1) identify which life process — nutrition or respiration — is disrupted; (2) name the structure or organ affected; (3) describe the immediate consequence of the disruption; (4) explain in one causal sentence why the disruption threatens the animal's survival.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use causal language in your final column — phrases such as 'because', 'so that', 'which means that', or 'without which'. Each row in the final column should begin with the disrupted process and end with the consequence for the animal's survival.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four columns filled for each scenario
One causal sentence per row in the final column

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scenario table requires students to classify each disruption by life process, identify the affected structure, and produce a justified causal explanation — making it the most direct demonstration vehicle for the final stage implied LO, which requires both identification and causal reasoning across nutrition and respiration. The teacher may substitute a predict-and-explain task or a procedure evaluation task using the same scenarios from the same menu.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences the student's ability to apply causal reasoning across both major life processes to novel animal scenarios, connecting structural disruption to downstream survival consequences — the chapter's highest cognitive operation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to use causal connectives rather than sequential ones; a teacher can assess the quality of reasoning by checking whether the final column goes beyond 'the animal cannot eat' to explain the mechanism: why not eating or not exchanging gases threatens survival. The frog scenario is the most demanding because it requires cross-referencing moist-skin respiration with the environmental condition discussed in unit eight.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly identify the life process in each row, name a specific structure, and write a causal sentence that chains disruption → consequence → survival threat using explicit connectives. Weak responses: correctly name the disrupted structure but describe consequences in sequential rather than causal language ('first this happens, then this happens'), or collapse nutrition and respiration into a generic 'the animal will die' without mechanistic justification.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find completing all four rows under time pressure difficult can be asked to complete two rows fully — one nutrition scenario and one respiration scenario — so that both life processes are still represented in their response. Students who struggle with written causal sentences can annotate the table with arrows connecting the disrupted organ to the downstream consequence, which demonstrates the same relational reasoning through a diagrammatic form.
